glossary.means: the corporate regulator. It licenses financial advice businesses, sets the guidance they work to, and bans people from the industry.
glossary.matters: an ASIC action is usually the item that changes what an adviser does, which is why these land as ACT.
glossary.check: asic.gov.au

glossary.means: the prudential regulator. It supervises banks, insurers and super funds for financial soundness, where ASIC watches conduct.
glossary.matters: an APRA item is usually about an institution's stability rather than about advice practice.
glossary.check: apra.gov.au

glossary.means: the free external complaints scheme. A consumer who cannot resolve a complaint with a firm can take it to AFCA, whose determination binds the firm.
glossary.matters: determinations show how obligations are read in a real dispute, which is why they sit in the ACT tier.
glossary.check: afca.org.au

glossary.means: the tribunal that reviews government decisions, including ASIC bannings. It replaced the Administrative Appeals Tribunal in October 2024.
glossary.matters: a ban can be affirmed, varied or set aside here, so an ASIC decision is not always the last word.
glossary.check: art.gov.au

glossary.means: the tax administrator, and the regulator of self-managed super funds.
glossary.matters: it is the primary source for how a tax or SMSF rule is actually applied, ahead of any commentary about it.
glossary.check: ato.gov.au

glossary.means: the main professional association for advisers, formed in 2023 from the merger of the FPA and the AFA.
glossary.matters: it speaks for the profession in consultations. That is a position, not a rule — useful context, rarely an obligation.
glossary.check: faaa.au

glossary.means: a scheme that pays limited compensation to a consumer who has won an AFCA determination the firm has not paid.
glossary.matters: it is funded by a levy on licensees, so changes to how it works change what advice businesses pay.
glossary.check: cslr.org.au, and Treasury for any change to the levy

glossary.means: the licence a business must hold to provide financial services. An adviser either holds one or is authorised under someone else's.
glossary.matters: the licensee carries the obligations, so who holds the licence decides who is answerable.
glossary.check: asic.gov.au

glossary.means: a person or business authorised to provide financial services under another entity's licence.
glossary.matters: it explains why a story about one adviser is often a story about their licensee.
glossary.check: asic.gov.au, and ASIC Connect's professional registers

glossary.means: an ASIC order stopping a person from providing financial services, or controlling a financial services business, for a set period or permanently.
glossary.matters: the reasons given are the closest thing to a worked example of how conduct obligations are applied.
glossary.check: the media release and the banning notice at asic.gov.au

glossary.means: the legal duty to act in the client's best interests when giving personal advice, in the Corporations Act.
glossary.matters: most advice enforcement comes back to it, so it is worth knowing in its own words rather than in summary.
glossary.check: the Corporations Act on legislation.gov.au, and ASIC's guidance

glossary.means: the ethical standards binding financial advisers, covering competence, honesty, fairness and conflicts of interest.
glossary.matters: it sits alongside the law rather than inside it: conduct can meet the Act and still breach the Code.
glossary.check: legislation.gov.au for the instrument, asic.gov.au for how breaches are handled

glossary.means: the government's package of advice reforms, following the Quality of Advice Review — simplifying advice documents and obligations, and proposing a new class of adviser.
glossary.matters: it is the source of most reform talk in the trade press. Much of it is proposed, not law.
glossary.check: treasury.gov.au — and confirm whether a measure is announced, in draft, or in force

glossary.means: the document that sets out personal advice, the reasons for it, and what it costs.
glossary.matters: changes to it are a live reform topic, so check whether a description is current or proposed.
glossary.check: treasury.gov.au for reform status, asic.gov.au for what is required today

glossary.means: the prohibition on offering a financial product to a consumer during, or because of, unsolicited contact.
glossary.matters: it decides how a firm may approach someone who did not ask, including through referrals.
glossary.check: the Corporations Act and ASIC's regulatory guidance

glossary.means: a payment that could reasonably influence advice given to a client. Most forms of it are banned.
glossary.matters: it is the rule behind most stories about commissions and adviser payments.
glossary.check: the Corporations Act and ASIC's guidance

glossary.means: the obligation on a licensee to report certain breaches, and likely breaches, to ASIC within set timeframes.
glossary.matters: the reporting numbers ASIC publishes are where a lot of enforcement attention starts.
glossary.check: asic.gov.au regulatory guidance

glossary.means: the duty on product issuers and distributors to design a product for a defined group of consumers and distribute it to that group.
glossary.matters: it is the obligation behind the target market determination attached to a product.
glossary.check: asic.gov.au regulatory guidance

glossary.means: the document saying which consumers a financial product is designed for, and how it may be distributed.
glossary.matters: distributing outside it is the breach ASIC acts on, so the document is the test.
glossary.check: the product issuer's own TMD, and asic.gov.au

glossary.means: the disclosure document for a financial product — what it is, its risks, and its costs.
glossary.matters: it is the primary source for what a product actually does, ahead of any description of it.
glossary.check: the issuer's current PDS

glossary.means: a superannuation fund run by its own members, who are also its trustees and carry the legal responsibility.
glossary.matters: the trustee obligations, and the ATO's role as regulator, are what separate these from other funds.
glossary.check: ato.gov.au

glossary.means: a proposed additional tax on earnings attributable to very large superannuation balances.
glossary.matters: its thresholds, start date and mechanics have changed more than once. Nothing about it should be taken from a summary.
glossary.check: treasury.gov.au and ato.gov.au for the current status — confirm before relying on any figure

glossary.means: the obligation on super fund trustees to have a strategy for helping members in retirement, not just while they are saving.
glossary.matters: it is why funds have moved into retirement guidance, which touches what advisers do.
glossary.check: apra.gov.au and asic.gov.au

glossary.means: the supervised year a new adviser completes before advising independently, with structured training and a supervisor.
glossary.matters: for someone entering the industry this is the path itself, not background.
glossary.check: asic.gov.au and the FAAA's guidance for new entrants

glossary.means: the ongoing training an adviser must complete each year to stay authorised.
glossary.matters: the requirement is set by law and topped up by the licensee, so counts and categories vary.
glossary.check: asic.gov.au, then your licensee's own policy

glossary.means: a firm's own complaints process, which a consumer uses before AFCA.
glossary.matters: the timeframes and record-keeping are prescribed, and failures here show up in AFCA determinations.
glossary.check: asic.gov.au regulatory guidance

glossary.means: insurance cover that pays where a person is permanently unable to work, usually to a definition set in the policy.
glossary.matters: the definition in the policy decides the claim, and definitions differ between products.
glossary.check: the policy document, and the Life Insurance Code of Practice

glossary.means: the life insurance industry's own code, with a committee that monitors it and can sanction a breaching insurer.
glossary.matters: a code sanction is industry self-regulation, not a regulator's action. Both matter; they are not the same thing.
glossary.check: the code at fsc.org.au, and asic.gov.au for anything regulatory

glossary.means: a client who meets asset or income tests and so receives fewer protections than a retail client.
glossary.matters: the tests, and whether they should change, are a live policy argument. Which category a client is in changes the obligations owed.
glossary.check: the Corporations Act, and treasury.gov.au for any review

glossary.means: an arrangement where a client's portfolio is managed to a model, with the client holding the underlying assets.
glossary.matters: it changes how advice is implemented and reviewed, which is why platform stories dwell on it.
glossary.check: the offer document, and asic.gov.au on the licensing of the service

glossary.means: the total value of money a manager or platform looks after.
glossary.matters: it is a size and momentum figure, not a quality one. Useful as market context, rarely more.
glossary.check: the manager's own reporting

glossary.means: the tax on a gain made when an asset is sold or otherwise disposed of.
glossary.matters: concessions and exemptions do a lot of work here, and they are specific. Never take one from a summary.
glossary.check: ato.gov.au

items.title: ASIC lifts stop orders against Remara
items.teaser: ASIC has lifted three interim stop orders against Remara Investment Management's private credit products, after it amended its target market determination (TMD).
items.brief_text: ASIC has lifted three interim stop orders against Remara Investment Management's private credit products , after it amended its target market determination (TMD). Last week, the corporate watchdog claimed the products were too risky for retail investors. The three products - the 6 Month (Fixed and Variable) Account, 12 Month (Fixed and Variable) Account and At Call Account - sit under the Remara Cash Management Fund, a registered managed investment scheme. ASIC had hit Remara and its trustee Melbourne Securities Corporation (MSC) with the interim design distribution orders (DDO) stop orders for 21 days unless revoked earlier. Amendments made by Remara addressed ASIC's concerns by removing 'capital preservation' as a suitable investment objective and introducing a new category of 'low capital volatility'. It also amended the rating of the consumer's risk and return profile from low to a rating of medium and potentially low to medium. The fund removed generalised access-to-capital categories and replaced them with categories specific to the products, which consider the redemption timeframes under its constitution. It also reduced the percentage of investor's investable assets considered to be appropriate for investment in the products from 'major component' (up to 75%) and 'core component' (up to 50%) to 'minor' (up to 25%) and 'satellite' (up to 10%). ASIC recommended investors in the products to review whether they remain suitable for their financial objectives, situation or needs. ASIC's surveillance of private credit funds includes targeting the distribution of private credit funds to retail clients through direct and advised channels, as well as examining fees, margin structures and conflict-of-interest management in wholesale private credit funds. Last week, the corporate regulator urged the private credit sector to uplift standards, noting participants should prepare for enforcement action if they fail to do so.

items.title: BRP definition still causing confusion in LRBA rules
items.teaser: There is still confusion around the new limited recourse borrowing arrangement rules and what property SMSFs are now allowed to borrow for, Leigh Mansell, Director SMSF Technical and Education for Heffron, said.
items.brief_text: There is still confusion around the new limited recourse borrowing arrangement rules and what property SMSFs are now allowed to borrow for, Leigh Mansell, Director SMSF Technical and Education for Heffron, said. “Basically the rules say a fund is only allowed to borrow to acquire a property using an LRBA if that property is business real property and this is where we’re hearing a lot of people getting a little bit confused,” Mansell said. “They’re just hearing that it is a ban on residential property, but it is essentially a ban on anything that’s not business real property. That would put residential property in the ban bucket, but it might put other things in the ban bucket as well.” Mansell said the new law means an SMSF is not allowed to borrow to acquire any real property unless the property is business real property. “A lot of people would be familiar with the definition of business real property. It lives in the super law, and is essentially real property used wholly and exclusively in one or more businesses. It doesn’t need to be your client’s business. It could be anybody’s business,” she said. “There’s a definitional change to what business real property actually is. We’ve got a SIS definition of what it is. We’ve also got an ATO ruling from 2009 that gives us the ATO’s interpretation of what it means within the definition within SIS of some of the elements of the definition. “One of the elements within the definition of business real property is all about the real property being used wholly and exclusively in one or more businesses. In a 2009 SMSF ruling, the ATO expressed its interpretation of what is meant by wholly and exclusively.” She continued that if looking at the legislation in isolation, many people would believe a property may meet the definition of BRP, but it is important to remember that the property must be used wholly and exclusively for business purposes at all times. “Otherwise, it’s not going to meet the business real property definition. The ATO definition is not that black and white. It said that if a bit of that property is not being used at all, so there might be just a small chunk of it not being used at all, the ATO has basically said in that case, as long as the property is being used to an appreciable degree in one or more businesses, it won’t fail to meet the definition of business real property,” she said. “There’s also another limb within the ruling from the ATO, and it also identifies that there might be some non-business use, and sometimes the non-business use might be ‘mission critical’ in relation to the person using the property for the purposes of running their business.” For example, she said, a motel that requires someone to live on site 24/7. “There’s a non-business use to that person living on site as part and parcel of the motel business, the ATO has recognised in the ruling that this kind of situation is mission critical for that motel business to run. That wouldn’t be a problem from a business real property definition.” she said. “The ATO has also recognised that some minor, trifling, insignificant non-business use would also not jeopardize the property meeting the business real property definition. There’s also another thing when we’re dealing with businesses that are primary production properties being used in somebody’s primary production business. “There’s a little exemption whenever one of those primary production properties has a piece of it being used for private or domestic purposes. The law in this case, has a safe harbor, that says it’s okay for a primary production business to have a dwelling as long as the dwelling doesn’t take up more than two hectares, and it’s not the predominant use of the property.”

items.title: Clime suspended from ASX for missing audit deadline
items.teaser: Clime Investment Management has been suspended from the ASX after it missed the September 30 deadline to lodge its audited annual report.
items.brief_text: Clime Investment Management has been suspended from the ASX after it missed the September 30 deadline to lodge its audited annual report. Trading in Clime will remain suspended until after the FY26 annual report is released on the ASX. "While this is disappointing, the board is not aware of any material change to the preliminary financial report published on 31 August 2026," Clime said. It expects to release the audited reports in the coming days. Clime said estimated pre-tax profit remains at $1 million, with the board intending to declare a fully franked dividend of 50 cents per share on completion of the audit. Clime recently said it is selling its separately managed accounts (SMA) products and some managed funds for about $7.7 million to an unnamed party. "Commercial terms are agreed. These transactions represent further progress in exiting sub-scale retail product structures and aligning the group to its future mandate-led operating model," Clime said. The group has also finalised the sale of its retail advice arm, Clime Advice, for $6 million, comprising $1 million in equity and vendor finance of $5 million. It retains a 10% interest in the newly combined business. The Australian Financial Review recently reported Clime Private Wealth was barred from the Netwealth platform two months ago following a review. Clime Investment Management managing director Michael Baragwanath told Financial Standard the report is incorrect without providing further details. Clime Private Wealth chief executive Kieran Berry and Clime Investment Management executive director John Abernethy did not respond to requests for comment. A Netwealth spokesman said: "We will not comment on individual clients, advisers, or fund managers, and will not be drawn into specifics of any particular matter. What we can say is that our governance processes are designed to identify issues early, and our preference is always to work collaboratively with our platform stakeholders toward resolution."

items.title: APRA targets trustees with new investment rules
items.teaser: This comes as the industry continues to reel in the wake of alleged trustee misconduct, with First Guardian-linked Equity Trustees under the spotlight for its involvement in the collapse.
items.brief_text: This comes as the industry continues to reel in the wake of alleged trustee misconduct, with First Guardian-linked Equity Trustees under the spotlight for its involvement in the collapse. APRA said the changes will form the next phase of its multi-year focus on lifting regulatory and governance standards across the superannuation industry, especially within the trust segment. The proposals build on APRA’s supervisory and enforcement work and address shortcomings identified in its 2025 review of platform trustee practices. It said this will “strengthen requirements across eight key areas of risk and build on existing obligations for trustees”. Three new safeguards, according to APRA, would require trustees to: Set and enforce member-level investment limits for higher-risk investments; Strengthen the management of investment-related conflicts; and Ensure their investment oversight capabilities and resources are commensurate with the size and complexity of their investment menus. APRA is also proposing five additional changes to codify and strengthen existing expectations for investment onboarding, monitoring, remediation, valuations and accountability. Alongside the proposed investment governance reforms, APRA will continue its supervisory focus on platform trustees. As part of this work, APRA is considering whether certain remuneration requirements that currently apply to large trustees should also apply to complex trustees of all sizes to support effective and prudent governance. “Trustees are ultimately accountable for the investments they make available to members. Investment choice must be supported by consistently strong safeguards, rigorous oversight and timely action when risks emerge,” APRA deputy chair David Bradbury said. “The failures of Shield and First Guardian demonstrate the serious harm that can occur when members accumulate concentrated holdings in poor or unsuitable investment options”. He continued: “Despite extensive supervisory and enforcement activity, material weaknesses in trustees’ investment governance practices remain. Policy reform is needed to strengthen trustee accountability and help ensure members’ interests remain at the centre of investment decisions”. APRA expects these changes would apply to all trustees, with particular impact on platform trustees, “given their typically broader investment menus, more complex products and greater reliance on financial advisers and other third parties”. The regulator also said the proposals are in line with Financial Services Minister Dan Mulino’s August 19 reforms. As said before, APRA’s proposal comes alongside continued scrutiny of trustees and their involvement in the Shield and First Guardian collapses, including Equity Trustees, who recently appeared before a joint parliamentary committee last month. At the hearing, Michael O’Brien, managing director of Equity Trustees and non-executive director Catherine Robson defended the trustees’ conduct in relation to Shield and First Guardian. Despite this, ASIC has sued the company for $65 million over its alleged failures. Equity Trustees has also seen a 20 per cent hit to its profit due to its involvement in the saga. Another trustee embroiled in this saga is Diversa Trustees, who’s involvement with First Guardian has seen them come under formal investigation from APRA. Diversa has also faced its own scrutiny in front of the joint parliamentary committee, seemingly laying the blame on everyone else for recommending First Guadian to investors, including the fund itself and the platforms that distributed the fund (Praemium and OneView Wealth). “We appreciate that the government and the parliament are determined to learn lessons from First Guardian to make sure a collapse like this doesn’t happen again. That’s exactly what we want too, and we want the opportunity to contribute,” Diversa independent director and chair Vincent Plant said in his opening statement. Defending their position, the group argued that they followed the procedures of the time which they thought to be sufficient to assess the suitability of a fund prior to its acceptance onto the platform.

items.title: Card surcharges are banned from October 1. What’s changing at the checkout?
items.teaser: Australians use debit and credit cards to pay for almost three out of four payments. Here’s what will soon change for shoppers and businesses.
items.brief_text: From October 1 this year, businesses will be banned from adding a surcharge when customers pay with a debit, credit, EFTPOS or prepaid card. The Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association has said it “will be one of the largest changes in payments” in Australia’s history – and many small businesses “are unprepared for its arrival”. The change follows a lengthy Reserve Bank of Australia review and decision to remove surcharging from all designated card networks (EFTPOS, Mastercard and Visa). American Express is voluntarily joining the change. When the Reserve Bank first effectively allowed card surcharges in 2003 , Australians mostly paid in cash. Cash still accounted for 69% of payments in 2007, when the central bank first began tracking payment methods usage. Back then, debit and credit cards were used for only one in four payments . Now, cards make up almost three out of four payments . Debit cards are Australians’ favourite way to pay, making up 49% of all payments in 2025, while credit cards came second, used for 23% of payments. Here’s what will change for shoppers, and what businesses will and won’t be allowed to charge at the checkout. What paying by card costs now Every time you pay with your card, it costs the business money to accept it. The current cost varies : 0.43% for an EFTPOS debit card, to about 1% for Visa or Mastercard credit cards, up to 1.36% for an American Express credit cards. Without the ability to add on a card surcharge, a business owner will have two choices: absorb the remaining cost themselves, or build those costs into slightly higher prices – passing the costs on to all customers, regardless of how they pay. Where customers will see changes Assuming some businesses do pass costs on to customers, shoppers regularly using cash can expect to see the biggest difference, given they can currently avoid card surcharges. Cash made up around 15% of consumer payments in 2025, but it’s used for almost one in four purchases under $10 . If you’re shopping at most large retailers – such as Woolworths, Coles or JB Hi-Fi – there shouldn’t be any difference from October 1. Most large businesses don’t currently apply card surcharges at the checkout. The change is more likely to be noticeable when buying from the 16% of businesses that have had card surcharges, including Aldi supermarkets, local grocers, cafes, restaurants, some tradespeople and some online stores.

Class actions muddy waters for AFCA, CSLR complaints
items.teaser: The past two weeks have seen both Macquarie and Netwealth served class actions over member losses related to Shield and First Guardian, despite both agreeing to restore actual losses last year in the order of $321 million and $101 million, respectively.
items.brief_text: The past two weeks have seen both Macquarie and Netwealth served class actions over member losses related to Shield and First Guardian, despite both agreeing to restore actual losses last year in the order of $321 million and $101 million , respectively. These claims are now looking to recoup unrealised or ‘but for’ losses, which has been met with mixed responses from across various stakeholders . Netwealth said it will defend the class action ; there has been no public response provided by Macquarie. Meanwhile, ifa understands it has created confusion as to what it will mean for AFCA complaints and the CSLR as it does introduce uncertainty when so many complaints have or are being lodged in relation to Shield and First Guardian, and the ramifications as yet are unknown. Attempting to provide some clarity, AFCA released a statement on 30 September saying it could impact some investors’ claims, but it depends on the individual circumstances. “AFCA acknowledges that these class actions may create confusion for consumers about what it means for their AFCA complaint – whether you have already lodged an AFCA complaint, or whether you intend to do so,” it stated. “These class actions are separate from the AFCA process, and they don’t automatically impact or prevent consumers from having a complaint with AFCA. Whether a class action affects an AFCA complaint depends on the circumstances of the individual complaint, including the issues raised and entities involved. “Many of the complaints lodged with AFCA in relation to Shield and First Guardian are about the financial advice consumers received. However, if the same loss is claimed in both the class actions and the particular AFCA complaint, we will consider the class actions and the implications for consumers.” The trouble is that some impacted Macquarie or Netwealth members may not know they are part of the class action and as AFCA understands, there is “no opportunity to opt-in or opt-out of the proceedings at this stage”. This means the actual scope of the matter is hard to pin down, though Gordon Legal, the lawyers behind the Macquarie class action, said in its initial announcement that they were representing around 2,800 account holders. “AFCA considers the circumstances of each complaint individually,” AFCA said. “If your complaint relates to the financial advice that you received, we will be in contact if there is any overlap with the class action, or implications for your complaint. We are currently progressing these complaints as per AFCA’s normal process.” Now the question is, what does it mean for advisers and the CSLR? In theory, a successful class action would mean fewer claims going through the CSLR, which means a smaller bill for advisers. And after Treasury announced that advisers could be on the hook for another $10 million through the FY27 special levy, anything that can be done to shrink the next one probably sounds quite appealing. However, ifa understands there is also concerns about future implications if the case is successful as there are currently several matters going through proceedings in relation to Shield and First Guardian; Diversa , Equity Trustees , SQM Research, MWL Financial Services and InterPrac Financial Planning , to name a few. These cases are already proving highly complex and timelines for court dates stretch well into next year. On top of this, there are thousands of AFCA complaints progressing through the system related to the collapses, including 1,396 against InterPrac in FY2025-026 and more continue to pour in.

With the RBA cash rate now at 4.6 per cent, Oliver explains why the central bank has moved to reinforce its inflation-fighting credibility, and why mortgage holders are bearing more of the burden than households benefiting from higher deposit rates. items.title: SMSF auditors should take note of ATO focus
items.teaser: Panagis said, following a recent roundtable, the ATO has stated that Division 296 won’t change the existing obligations of an SMSF auditor but they should be aware of two key issues going forward. “The first one is market valuations.
items.brief_text: Panagis said, following a recent roundtable, the ATO has stated that Division 296 won’t change the existing obligations of an SMSF auditor but they should be aware of two key issues going forward. “The first one is market valuations. The ATO is saying that auditors should ensure that there is sufficient and appropriate evidence to support the market value of assets, and where that evidence can’t be obtained, then consideration should be given to modifying the independent auditor’s report,” Panagis said. “The second item is all about making sure of fair and reasonable allocation of earnings. Auditors are reminded that trustees must allocate investment earnings to members on a fair and reasonable basis in accordance with the SIS requirements. Where this isn’t satisfied, auditors have been reminded they may need to modify their auditor’s report.” Panagis continued that it’s important SMSF auditors remember that fair and reasonable allocation of earnings doesn’t mean those earnings of accounts are going to match the share of Div 296 earnings. “That’s because the SMSF’s Div 296 earnings will be calculated differently to the net earnings of the fund for the purposes of the annual accounts. For example, the SMSF Div 296 earnings would use adjusted cost basis for the calculations of any realised capital gains,” she said. “For that reason, the earnings that are reported in the member statements may differ slightly or significantly from the earnings that are used to calculate a member’s Div 296 tax liability.” Panagis continued the ATO has also indicated it will also be looking to ensure auditors are complying with the updated guidance. “The main thing is all about updated auditor guidance, so confirming the unreimbursed SMSF establishment costs, and just reminding them that that will not lead to a contribution. Then there was also some updated guidance on crypto assets,” she said. “This mainly came about because there were a number of issues auditors were facing in terms of getting sufficient evidence for ownership, existence, valuation, control of these assets. Other things it is focusing on is audit quality and valuation evidence. “This is where the ATO is going to continue to focus on identifying deficiencies in asset ownership, market valuations, related party transactions, charges. That’s still going to be important for the ATO but the key thing here is market evaluation compliance and particularly with Div 296 now in play. “Finally, auditor independence is another key one that remains a primary enforcement priority for the ATO. It will also be looking at in-house audit arrangements as well and have said it will take stronger regulatory action where independence requirements are breached.”

items.title: ASIC’s ‘guide’ for advisers considering private credit funds
items.teaser: ASIC’s 10 principles for “private credit done well” provide a timely and useful roadmap for financial advisers considering whether exposure to the asset class is right for clients.
items.brief_text: Melbourne Securities Corporation’s Remara Cash Management Fund was self-assessed as low-risk and marketed as suitable for up to 75 per cent of a retail portfolio. ASIC disagreed. On 22 September, the regulator issued interim stop orders against three of the fund’s products, saying its target market determination (TMD) was deficient and that retail investors risked being sold something that did not suit their objectives, financial situation or needs. At a Commercial & Asset Finance Brokers of Australia (CAFBA) summit in Sydney last week, ASIC Commissioner Simone Constant said private credit governance, controls and underwriting standards have not kept pace with the sector’s growth, and that the regulator is now well beyond warnings. ASIC has multiple enforcement investigations underway and is running active surveillance across wholesale and retail funds, she said. ASIC published 10 principles for “private credit done well” in Report 823: Advancing Australia’s evolving capital markets , covering stewardship, governance, transparency, fees, conflicts of interest, valuations, liquidity and credit risk. Constant said she expects boards and investment committees to use the principles as a benchmark for self-assessment and to embed them into decision-making, not treat them as optional. She asked how many boardrooms and investment committees had actually discussed the principles or built them into their own decision-making, and if not, why not. If a manager has not assessed its fund against them, or will not say whether it has, that is the first red flag. “As a starting point, we articulated a set of 10 principles of private credit done well – to assist industry in understanding ‘what good looks like’,” Constant said. “Our expectation is that firms use these principles as a practical benchmark for self-assessment and uplift. And we expect boards and investment committees to consider how funds measure up against them and to embed the 10 principles into their decision-making. “And so, I ask the question… : How many of you have discussed these principles in your own boardrooms or investment committees? How many of you have embedded these into your own decision-making? And if not, why not?” Constant said some of the poorer practices across the industry – including “opaque remuneration and fee structures, inadequate governance arrangements, poor valuation practices, ineffective disclosure” – were “concerning and demanded scrutiny”. Constant said ASIC reviewed 28 private credit funds and found only four disclosed the interest rates charged to borrowers. Less than half had adequate credit or default management policies, and most had no separation between the people approving loans and the people assessing their ongoing performance, she said. “Less than half had detailed credit or impairment and default management policies in place. Most funds did not have adequate separation between those approving loans and those responsible for independently assessing their ongoing performance and value. And of the wholesale funds, only two performed stress testing as part of their liquidity risk management. “These were clearly red flags, particularly when we think… about the critical risks to be managed in private credit – credit and liquidity risk – and the fundamental importance of course, of effective disclosure when we’re seeing such a widespread growth in the sector.” Only two of the wholesale funds stress-tested their liquidity risk. Constant said these were clear warning signs, given how much rides on credit risk, liquidity risk and effective disclosure in a fast-growing sector. Offering regular redemptions against illiquid, multi-year property loans creates a fragile product design that breaks down under pressure. Clarity is needed on borrower arrears, interest capitalisation, developer exposures and the exact rules governing redemption queues before a client’s capital, or their access to it, is at risk. Constant said the collapse of Bathla showed $3.4 billion from more than 40 lenders funnelled through around 540 special purpose vehicles (SPVs). Related-party arrangements and SPVs can hide conflicts of interest that even sophisticated investors do not see, she said. If a manager cannot explain the structure in plain terms, do not recommend the product until they can. Constant said real estate lending makes up 40 to 60 per cent, or more, of Australian private credit. Property is not the weakest link, poor practice is, she said, but a fund concentrated in construction and development lending needs deal selection, counterparty diversification and liquidity buffers that match the cycle it is exposed to. Constant said ASIC welcomed the Financial Services Council’s Private Markets Best Practice Standards, released in August, as a constructive first step. It is a second, industry-built reference point to check a manager against, alongside ASIC’s 10 principles. ASIC’s 10 principles for private credit funds done well 1. Stewards of other people’s money Responsible entities and trustees act as stewards of investor capital, ensuring that their decisions are fair and in investors’ best interests. 2. Organisational capability Human, financial and technological resources are adequate. REs and trustees operate efficiently, honestly and fairly. 3. Transparency Investors have access to timely, transparent information on investment strategy, exposures, valuations, risks and fees. 4. Design and distribution Design and distribution practices are fair, transparent and appropriately targeted for investors. 5. Fees and costs Fees and costs are fair and transparent, giving investors and borrowers a clear view of total costs. 6. Conflicts of interest Conflicts of interest are identified, disclosed and effectively managed or avoided. 7. Governance Structures, processes and people promote sound decision-making, compliance and accountability. 8. Valuations Valuations are fair, timely and transparent, with robust governance. 9. Liquidity Liquidity risk is effectively disclosed and managed, avoiding structural mismatches, with fair redemption terms aligned to portfolio liquidity. 10. Credit risk Credit risk is effectively managed across loan origination, portfolio construction, monitoring, impairment, default and repayment. Source: Report 823: Advancing Australia’s evolving capital markets

items.title: Paraplanning’s Next Era: Strategic, Tech-Driven, Compliance-Led
items.teaser: Silvia Wade Founder of Mutual Paraplanning Services Paraplanning’s Next Era: Strategic, Tech Driven, Compliance Led For a long time, people in our profession have viewed paraplanners as note-takers and creators…
items.brief_text: Silvia Wade Founder of Mutual Paraplanning Services Paraplanning’s Next Era: Strategic, Tech Driven, Compliance Led For a long time, people in our profession have viewed paraplanners as note-takers and creators of Statements of Advice only after the strategy is set. But times have changed. That old view no longer reflects the present, or future of paraplanning. The modern paraplanner is both a strategic partner and a compliance gatekeeper within the advice preparation process As AI automation and other technology become the norm, the role of paraplanners is evolving in exciting ways. Technology is removing the repetitive, process-driven parts of our work, creating space for experienced paraplanners to become more strategic, proactive, and valuable to advice practices. And as AI accelerates meeting notes, data organisation, and SOA preparation, it frees paraplanners to focus on higher-value work. After all, an SOA is merely a format for delivering advice; it is not the advice itself. Someone must understand the client, explore suitable strategies, model outcomes, conduct research, and ensure the recommendations can be supported. That deeper work is where today’s paraplanners can contribute most Empty heading Strategic support and modelling The modern paraplanner can analyse, model, question, research, validate and collaborate. Rather than relying on templated SOA phrasing, they can incorporate strategic modelling and add “meat on the bone”, explaining why the recommendation matters to this particular person and what it could help them achieve. So, instead of an SOA simply saying a strategy “should” work, they can enable advisers to demonstrate how different decisions and assumptions may affect the outcome, ultimately turning complex client circumstances into clear, highly-personalised advice that clearly connects with the client’s goals. That is very different from note-taking or simple SOA documentation. Empty heading Compliance gate-keeping An experienced, knowledgeable paraplanner can also embed compliance throughout the advice creation process. They can work within the practice’s licensee requirements, ensure strategy and product research is properly captured, identify missing information, flag areas that require further clarification, and thoroughly document the assumptions, alternatives, and reasoning supporting a recommendation — making certain the work is accurate, defensible, complete, and ready for scrutiny from a compliance perspective. Empty heading Providing the deeper support that today’s increasingly complex financial advice demands At the same time as these technological changes are emerging, the advice many Australians need is becoming more sophisticated and less “vanilla”. We are seeing demand from pre-retirees in their 40s exploring whether they can retire earlier, retirees seeking greater certainty, high-net-worth clients navigating tax strategies, and families planning intergenerational wealth transfers. These clients may have assets held in different entities, competing goals, and future events to consider. Advisers in this space don’t simply need a paraplanner to take an order and turn it into a document. They need an equally capable second set of eyes, and second brain behind them: a paraplanner who can help formulate strategies, conduct product research, identify gaps, use models and projections to compare different scenarios and quantify the effect each may have on the client’s future. For example: What happens if the client retires two years earlier? How could a future inheritance affect the strategy? What if investment returns or living expenses differ from the original assumption? Which option produces the strongest outcome, and what trade-offs come with it? Is there another strategy that has not yet been considered Delivering this depth of support and modelling, while helping advisers deliver compliant advice to clients, is where the future value of paraplanning lies – and it’s why experienced paraplanners are assets to advisers. Empty heading From transactional support to a lasting partnership I believe AI advancements may shift the economics of paraplanning, and lead the industry to value experienced onshore paraplanning once again – because as technology handles more repetitive work, the key distinction will move away from labour cost to the depth of value provided. Rather than relying on support focused solely on creating documents, advisers may increasingly seek those paraplanners who intimately understand the Australian advice environment, proactively gatekeep compliance, and contribute strategically. This type of partnership helps advisers deliver stronger advice, reduce rework, increase output, support more clients, and scale their practice. And when a partnership like that is built over the long term, a paraplanner learns how an adviser thinks, how their practice operates, and what standards the business requires. That knowledge compounds over time. As technology takes care of more of the mechanics, the human value of paraplanning becomes easier to see: judgement, experience, strategic thinking and prompting, and a deep understanding of both the adviser and their clients. This is the future of paraplanning – and it’s a future I’m excited to help lead. Silvia Wade is the Founder and Director of Mutual Plans , a multi award winning outsourced, onshore paraplanning services provider for financial planners.
items.ai_summary: • Modern paraplanners are now strategic partners and compliance gatekeepers, not just note-takers

items.title: APRA expects proposed reforms to hit platforms hardest
items.teaser: APRA has proposed requiring super trustees to limit members' exposure to high-risk investment options as part of a package the regulator expects to have the greatest impact on platform trustees following the $1 billion collapse of Shield and First Guardian.
items.brief_text: APRA has proposed requiring superannuation trustees to set and enforce limits on members’ exposure to high-risk investment options as part of a package of investment governance reforms it expects to fall most heavily on platform trustees. The proposals, released for consultation on Wednesday, would apply to all trustees, but APRA deputy chair David Bradbury told a media briefing that the regulator expected platforms to feel the greatest effect. “All of these rules will affect all superannuation trustees, but I think it is worth acknowledging that they are expected to have the greatest impact on platform trustees,” Bradbury said, noting the breadth of investments platforms typically offer, the complexity of some of those products, and platforms’ greater reliance on third parties such as advisers. The proposals follow the $1 billion collapse of Shield and First Guardian master funds, which Bradbury described as “examples of where we see the severity of member harm that can be felt, where investment governance practices may not meet the standards or expectations that APRA would have”. He said APRA’s supervisory and enforcement work in recent years, including a thematic review and targeted enforcement action, had not fully addressed weaknesses in the sector. Under the proposals, trustees would set member-level limits on “concentrated higher-risk options”, subject to a ceiling set by APRA. The paper gives APRA’s preliminary view that a cap of 20 to 30 per cent per option, or group of options, may be appropriate. APRA expects trustees to set lower limits in many cases, the paper says, particularly for illiquid options such as private credit and for single ASX 300 securities. The limits would apply when a member buys into or adds to an investment. Existing holdings that grow past a limit would not generally have to be sold. Bradbury said the limits were intended to reduce the risk of members losing most or all of their retirement savings through concentrated positions. “It’s the difference between having an impact, a general impact on your super fund balance, or seeing it disappear completely,” he said. “So it’s not about eliminating choice; it’s really about putting some guardrails around choice.” Conflicts and clawbacks The package also proposes strengthening trustees’ management of conflicts of interest and requiring trustees to have the resources and capabilities needed to oversee their investment menus. Under the proposals, trustees would be required to identify and manage or avoid conflicts involving promoters, advisers and other third parties, and would also have to set and regularly review limits on the size and complexity of their investment menus, relative to their capability and resources. The proposals come amidst a broad push by profit-to-member funds and their proxies, including the Super Members Council, for governance uplift among the retail platforms to which they are losing an increasing number of members. In November 2025, the SMC proposed the expansion of the Financial Accountability Regime across all super and investment platforms and the reintroduction of ASIC’s “investing between the flags” initiative, which would see consumers warned when they are moving outside of system safeguards. The SMC also welcomed a proposed “cooling-off” period for super switching, which is widely seen as one way of slowing outflows to retail platforms. APRA is also considering whether remuneration requirements under CPS 511 that currently apply to significant financial institutions, including clawbacks, should be extended to complex super trustees, though Bradbury said that no decision had been made. “We’re not proposing that as policy change as part of this package,” Bradbury said. “I’ll make a general observation, and that is that it would seem appropriate that remuneration settings, and particularly those that relate to variable compensation, bear a relationship with the performance of the entity and whether or not the entity is delivering for the best financial interests of its members, and I think that we want to ensure that the overall policy settings are such that there is an alignment between those considerations.” Bradbury said the proposals were separate from the government’s announcement last month on streamlining compensation arrangements, but were aligned in their objectives and would be complementary in effect. “All trustees are ultimately responsible for the investments that they offer their members,” he said.

items.title: ASIC cracking down on insurers over basic service failures
items.teaser: In its 2026-27 priorities, ASIC said it will focus on improving consumer outcomes within the life insurance sector after persistent failures within the sector.
items.brief_text: In its 2026-27 priorities, ASIC said it will focus on improving consumer outcomes within the life insurance sector after persistent failures within the sector. “Central to providing good service to customers is getting the basics right, which for an insurer includes retaining a copy of the insurance policy, calculating premiums correctly and paying out the right benefits,” it stated. “Data from complaints and breaches reported to ASIC continues to suggest that these basic services are a significant cause of issues and concern for consumers.” ASIC is currently conducting a review into service issues in life insurance with the resulting report due early next year. Noting the important role life insurance plays in the lives and financial security of Australians, ASIC said providers in this sector may also be rolled into broader reviews, such as its financial reporting surveillance. They may also be in scope for phase three of the regulator’s review of superannuation member services as many Australians access life insurance through their super. While not included in this specific review, ASIC said funeral insurance is also driving reports from AFAC and consumer groups to the regulator regarding issues with this type of insurance, “particularly where costs exceed benefits”. “In light of these concerns, ASIC expects to review insurers’ practices related to funeral insurance in the second half of 2026–27”. Beyond this, ASIC will continue to focus on misconduct targeting vulnerable customers, cyber resilience, and the impact of AI usage within the life sector. At the same time, the regulator is also working with the Council of Life Insurers (CALI) to draft a new Life Insurance Code of Practice following an independent review. CALI will be releasing its response to the review later today. ASIC chair Sarah Court said: “ASIC is actively working to increase transparency, reduce unnecessary duplication and make regulatory processes easier to navigate while maintaining the quality and integrity of regulatory outcomes. We have a clear mandate from government to support growth and productivity and a responsibility to ensure our actions strengthen the economy and do not unnecessarily slow it. “The supervisory letters form part of a broader Council of Financial Regulators workstream, jointly led by ASIC and APRA, to improve how regulators coordinate, collect and share data and respond to the Treasurer’s request for a Better Regulation Roadmap for the financial sector. “The letters provide sector-specific visibility of ASIC’s supervisory priorities and areas of focus. This greater level of transparency will help regulated entities plan and allocate resources with confidence. We encourage boards and executives to carefully consider the issues highlighted in the letters so they can plan, allocate resources and focus attention accordingly”.

items.title: Super advice fee deductions face ASIC scrutiny
items.teaser: ASIC said its priorities will help trustees plan, allocate resources and focus attention on “the issues boards and executives should consider and act on in the year ahead”.
items.brief_text: ASIC said its priorities will help trustees plan, allocate resources and focus attention on “the issues boards and executives should consider and act on in the year ahead”. Addressing the industry broadly, ASIC stated that, with approximately $4.4 trillion of member savings under their control, trustees have a key role to play in Australia’s retirement and broader economic landscape. “In this context, ASIC remains focused on trustee conduct and its impact on members. ASIC’s recent sector reviews, discussed in detail below, continue to highlight that some trustees are not getting the basics right in supporting members and delivering the services they need,” the regulator said. “Trustees must continue to improve their skills, systems, and processes to meet their obligations and uphold the trust placed in them by the Australian public.” In response, the regulator said it will promote the improvement of member services through its multi-year review of compliance with laws governing contact centres and trustee administration practices. Highlighting work in this area it has already completed, ASIC drew attention to its recently published report on trustees progress in uplifting death benefits claim handling practices: Delivering on death benefits: Have super trustees stepped up? The report, according to ASIC, found that while many trustees have made positive inroads, many are still yet to implement recommendations handed down by the regulator. Of particular focus will be a crackdown on trustee oversight of advice fee deductions. “In June 2026, ASIC published the findings of its review into platform trustees’ oversight of potential risks to superannuation savings in Report 833 Safeguarding super: How well are platform trustees monitoring risks to retirement savings?” the regulator said. “Our review identified gaps in the monitoring of harmful advice fee charges, unusual fees and investment patterns, and high-risk superannuation switching activity. Concerningly, the review identified instances of regression in practices over the past two years since ASIC’s last review into advice fees.” ASIC urged all trustees, including non-platform ones, to review current processes against the better practices and principles identified in the report, stating that in light of the identified deficiencies, it plans to commence a review of trustee oversight of advice charges in the first half of 2026-27. According to chief executive of Fourth Line Joel Ronchi, advisers should expect greater scrutiny when it comes to clients paying for advice out of their super following ASIC’s increased focus on the practice. “It’s a little bit like the lottery. It’s not like every adviser is going to have to explain themselves once a year. It’s actually the reverse, which is like the lottery, and that is, you have to be selected to for this to be a situation,” Ronchi told ifa. “However, what’s happening is, they’re going from maybe a few hundred file reviews a year to a few 1000 file reviews a year, so the likelihood that someone’s going to get called up across the various trustees obviously increases.” Another area ASIC said will be of priority is the Retirement Income Covenant (RIC), stating it will “continue to monitor industry progress since the implementation of the RIC, and in the second half of FY27 undertake a review, which may include industry wide insight into certain practices core to better retirement outcomes”. The regulator also said it will continue to improve its range of free retirement tools on Moneysmart, as well as conduct a review of guidance on fee and cost disclosures.

items.title: What do the Macquarie, Netwealth class actions mean for AFCA complaints?
items.teaser: The past two weeks have seen both Macquarie and Netwealth served class actions over member losses related to Shield and First Guardian, despite both agreeing to restore actual losses last year in the order of $321 million and $101 million, respectively.
items.brief_text: The past two weeks have seen both Macquarie and Netwealth served class actions over member losses related to Shield and First Guardian, despite both agreeing to restore actual losses last year in the order of $321 million and $101 million , respectively. These claims are now looking to recoup unrealised or ‘but for’ losses, which has been met with mixed responses from across various stakeholders . Netwealth said it will defend the class action ; there has been no public response provided by Macquarie. Meanwhile, ifa understands it has created confusion as to what it will mean for AFCA complaints and the CSLR as it does introduce uncertainty when so many complaints have or are being lodged in relation to Shield and First Guardian, and the ramifications as yet are unknown. Attempting to provide some clarity, AFCA released a statement on 30 September saying it could impact some investors’ claims, but it depends on the individual circumstances. “AFCA acknowledges that these class actions may create confusion for consumers about what it means for their AFCA complaint – whether you have already lodged an AFCA complaint, or whether you intend to do so,” it stated. “These class actions are separate from the AFCA process, and they don’t automatically impact or prevent consumers from having a complaint with AFCA. Whether a class action affects an AFCA complaint depends on the circumstances of the individual complaint, including the issues raised and entities involved. “Many of the complaints lodged with AFCA in relation to Shield and First Guardian are about the financial advice consumers received. However, if the same loss is claimed in both the class actions and the particular AFCA complaint, we will consider the class actions and the implications for consumers.” The trouble is that some impacted Macquarie or Netwealth members may not know they are part of the class action and as AFCA understands, there is “no opportunity to opt-in or opt-out of the proceedings at this stage”. This means the actual scope of the matter is hard to pin down, though Gordon Legal, the lawyers behind the Macquarie class action, said in its initial announcement that they were representing around 2,800 account holders. “AFCA considers the circumstances of each complaint individually,” AFCA said. “If your complaint relates to the financial advice that you received, we will be in contact if there is any overlap with the class action, or implications for your complaint. We are currently progressing these complaints as per AFCA’s normal process.” Now the question is, what does it mean for advisers and the CSLR? In theory, a successful class action would mean fewer claims going through the CSLR, which means a smaller bill for advisers. And after Treasury announced that advisers could be on the hook for another $10 million through the FY27 special levy, anything that can be done to shrink the next one probably sounds quite appealing. However, ifa understands there is also concerns about future implications if the case is successful as there are currently several matters going through proceedings in relation to Shield and First Guardian; Diversa , Equity Trustees , SQM Research, MWL Financial Services and InterPrac Financial Planning , to name a few. These cases are already proving highly complex and timelines for court dates stretch well into next year. On top of this, there are thousands of AFCA complaints progressing through the system related to the collapses, including 1,396 against InterPrac in FY2025-026 and more continue to pour in.

items.title: TRIS is not retirement phase income stream
items.teaser: There are several “myths” around transition to retirement income stream (TRIS) which SMSF trustees should be aware of to ensure they meet compliance obligations, Aaron Dunn, CEO of Smarter SMSF, said.
items.brief_text: There are several “myths” around transition to retirement income stream (TRIS) which SMSF trustees should be aware of to ensure they meet compliance obligations, Aaron Dunn, CEO of Smarter SMSF, said. Dunn said the most important thing to remember in regard to a TRIS is that it is not a retirement phase income stream, and generally starts when a member still has preserved benefits, the earnings of which are still subject to taxation in the fund as they would normally be in an accumulation interest. Tim Miller, Head of Technical and Education for Smarter SMSF, said one of the most frequently misunderstood concepts around a TRIS is that it has to be linked to transfer balance cap. “You only need to reference a transfer balance cap when you’re talking about a retirement phase income stream, and so is why it is a little bit more misunderstood. It was quite messy when it first came in around 2016-17 that a TRIS does not automatically convert to an account-based pension when you satisfy a condition of release,” Miller said. “Instead, it becomes a transition to retirement in the retirement phase, and although we play around on the words of that a little bit, conceptually, what people have to understand is that when you have a TRIS, it will always be a TRIS. You don’t stop the pension and start something new. You just move it across.” Miller said that means that a TRIS is “transitioned” to retirement in the retirement phase, and subject to the condition that’s been met, the member may need to notify the trustee. “So, if the condition is retirement or permanent incapacity or terminal illness, then you would notify the trustee of that, and that would be the trigger for reporting and evaluations for T-bar purposes,” he said. Dunn added that there are essentially two events needed to trigger that transition and there does need to be a formal notification of what that trigger is for a TRIS to move into the retirement phase. Miller continued that then gives the member the capacity to partially commute the pension. “If you did start with an amount greater than the transfer balance cap, or there was significant growth whilst you had the income stream in operation, you would be able to commute back to what the general transfer balance cap or what your personal transfer balance cap was on the day that you notified the trustee of satisfying that condition,” he said. “The quirk being that if the condition of release is turning 65, there’s no notification point. So, you want to make sure that if turning 65 is your condition that moves you to the retirement phase, that your pension is below or at the general transfer balance cap on your 65th birthday, because that’s an automatic event.” Dunn added that it is an important distinction that SMSF members need to be across in so far that there is forward planning that needs to be done when they are going to commute to align themselves with the 65th birthday and what the transfer balance cap will be. “As soon as you get to your 65th birthday and one day, you now have an excess transfer balance amount, and would therefore be subject to a computation authority to have to deal with that,” he said.

items.title: Victims’ advocate: Investors could ‘end up with breadcrumbs’ in class action
items.teaser: A class action brought against Macquarie in its capacity as trustee of a platform that hosted the collapsed Shield master fund may take longer to settle and yield poorer results for investors than pursuing claims through AFCA and the CSLR, a leading victims’ advocate has warned.
items.brief_text: Shield and First Guardian investor advocate Melinda Kee says a class action against Macquarie Investment Management is likely to produce a worse outcome for victims of the collapsed Shield master fund than the path already open to them through the Australian Financial Complaints Authority and the Compensation Scheme of Last Resort. Gordon Legal commenced the class action in the Supreme Court of Victoria on 16 September, on behalf of representative plaintiff Rachelle Dessent and around 2800 investors who put about $321 million of their superannuation into the collapsed Shield Master Fund through Macquarie’s platform. It seeks additional compensation for investment growth these investors missed out on, and for distress suffered as a result of the collapses. Shield and First Guardian combined have left close to 11,000 investors with about $1.2 billion at risk. Another platform operator, Netwealth, compensated investors in another failed managed investment scheme, First Guardian, to the tune of $100 million on a similar basis. Earlier this week, Netwealth informed the ASX that it had received a letter from solicitors acting for a proposed representative plaintiff “alleging breaches of duties in connection with the offering and monitoring of certain First Guardian investment options available through the Netwealth Superannuation Master Fund”. It said the proposed claims relate to matters “previously addressed through Netwealth’s court-enforceable undertaking with ASIC and the compensation program completed in January 2026”. No proceedings have yet been filed. Kee says it is far from certain how long it will take to settle the Macquarie class action, and the amount of compensation that ultimately flows to Shield victims is equally uncertain. Kee says it is likely to be significantly less than investors might receive through AFCA. “Gordon Legal will take 20 to 25 per cent to repay the litigation funder that is financing the class action”, Kee tells Professional Planner . “Then they will take out their legal fees and expenses [and] the investors end up with the breadcrumbs.” Complaint against a trustee Gordon Legal says on its website it is taking action against Macquarie because investors themselves are unable to bring a complaint at AFCA against a trustee, but Kee says “the lawyers have to know that [investors] may not be able to file a complaint against the trustee, but they can file a complaint against the licensee, whom their financial adviser fell under, that gave them the advice to go into these funds”. “Macquarie and Netwealth stepped up before Christmas for these victims, and… let’s say they’ve given back their net investment to these victims. And the responsibility for the balance should fall on the licensee, who ultimately failed in their due diligence. Also, and I don’t believe the trustees should wear 100 per cent liability.” “Interprac still have PI insurance, and there is still a cross guarantee between Sequoia and Interprac. So it is very likely that there will be the funds… to compensate a good percentage of victims through those PI insurances, and then obviously there is the compensation scheme of last resort.” Kee says the average investor in Shield is down between $77,000 and $120,000 which is well below the scheme’s compensation cap. Some investors may be down more than the scheme is able to compensate. Investors tempted to join the class action in the hope of effectively being compensated twice for the same loss may be disappointed. Professional Planner understands that the current CSLR legislation does not provide for compensation from the scheme to be reduced by the amount of compensation received by an individual from other sources. Any offset in compensation must be set out in a determination issued by the Australian Financial Complaints Authority. In some cases the quantum of compensation an individual has received from outside AFCA is known to the authority when it makes a determination. But the outcome of a class action, which potentially could take many months or years to settle, is uncertain anyway, and may not be known to AFCA. In this situation it is conceivable that the authority might be forced to pause determinations until the outcome of a class action is known. CSLR chief executive officer David Berry tells Professional Planner the scheme is “still investigating the implications of a class action”. “We certainly know the intent is to ensure there’s no overpayment of compensation, or double payment,” Berry says. In a statement provided to Professional Planner , AFCA said that “a class action does not automatically prevent someone from making a complaint to AFCA”. “Whether there is any impact on an AFCA complaint depends on the circumstances of the individual complaint, including the issues raised and the parties involved,” it said. “AFCA has considerable experience dealing with complaints where a consumer may also have access to compensation through another process. “Where that is the case, an AFCA determination can take the potential for other compensation into account.”

items.title: Ord Minnett appoints CEO as Morris steps back after 36 years
items.teaser: Ord Minnett chief executive, Karl Morris, is to step back from leadership of the business and the firm has appointed his successor after a two-year search. Morris will move into the executive chair role in February but remain working at Ord Minnett.
items.brief_text: Ord Minnett chief executive, Karl Morris, is to step back from leadership of the business and the firm has appointed his successor after a two-year search. Morris will move into the executive chair role in February but remain working at Ord Minnett. He began working at Ords as a state manager in 1990 before becoming CEO and managing director in 2004 and was executive chair from 2009 to 2020 when it was taken over by Warwick Smith. In his place, Antony Shaw will join the firm this month as an executive director before commencing as chief executive in February 2027. He was previously chief executive of HSBC Australia and New Zealand for three years until 2025 where he spent 23 years across UK, Asia and the Middle East. Smith will depart the board when Morris steps back into the chair role. Morris said: “Antony brings global leadership experience to Ord Minnett, which will help drive growth across the whole business. He is very well respected and has decades of senior banking and finance experience, so we are thrilled he will lead our firm. “We are an Australian-owned wealth management firm, and Antony’s recent role as Australia & New Zealand CEO for international bank HSBC will bring incredibly valuable experience and insight for Ords as we continue to deliver for our clients. “Throughout the two-year search, we looked for an exceptionally talented leader who could bring a corporate-focused lens to Ords, with a proven track record of growth and success for clients. We believe we have found that leader in Antony and look forward to his leadership in the years to come.” Shaw added: “It is a privilege to lead an Australian-owned business with such a proud history and strong client-first culture. While the leadership will change in 2027, the focus remains the same: delivering first-class service for our clients and helping them achieve their goals. “It is clear to me there are significant opportunities across the board for Ords, particularly at a time when the advice industry in Australia is experiencing significant demand. “I recognise both the opportunities and challenges ahead, and I look forward to building on Karl Morris’ legacy as we take the firm into its next chapter,” he said.

items.title: Praemium CEO resigns
items.teaser: Praemium CEO Anthony Wamsteker has resigned from the platform with immediate effect. Current chief commercial offier, Denis Orrock, will become acting CEO while the firm seeks a successor for Wamsteker.
items.brief_text: Praemium CEO Anthony Wamsteker has resigned from the platform with immediate effect. Current chief commercial offier, Denis Orrock, will become acting CEO while the firm seeks a successor for Wamsteker. Wamsteker joined Praemium in 2020 and became CEO in May 2021, he has a three-month notice period and will be available to Orrock as he steps into the acting position. An ASX statement from Praemium said: “The board will undertake a formal process for recruitment of a new CEO with the help of an external search firm. Both internal and external candidates will be considered by the board for the permanent CEO role.” Chair Matthew Quinn, who took on the chair role from Barry Lewin last month, thanked Wamsteker for his tenure and pointed to a new path for Praemium focused on technology. Quinn joined the Praemium board in June 2026 as a non-executive director and was previously chair of Bravura Solutions from June 2023 to October 2025. He said: “Praemium is at an exciting and pivotal point. We are currently transforming our technology platform and over the next year we will progressively roll out the new platform to our clients. “This will include a suite of new functionality and product enhancements designed to improve client user experience and enhance their productivity.
