items.title: Super sector an important source of resilience: RBA
items.teaser: The Reserve Bank of Australia said the superannuation sector is an important source of stability for the financial sector, but warned liquidity risks remains.
items.brief_text: The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has released its latest Financial Stability Review, saying Australia has a "good degree of resilience". The RBA said private market activity in Australia has supported favourable business credit conditions over recent years and noted while the rapid growth in the domestic private credit market has been from a low base, concerns over credit quality raise more issues for investor protection than financial stability. "In sum, while cyclical domestic risks continue to be closely monitored, they are not assessed as posing systemic financial stability risks at present," it said. On the superannuation sector, the RBA said it is important that as the sector grows, its liquidity risk management practices continue to strengthen to maintain resilience. The central bank also noted operation resilience requires ongoing action. "Improving operational resilience has become a prominent focus of regulators, banks, FMIs, superannuation funds and other financial institutions. This includes the development of robust contingency and recovery plans and crisis response capabilities. There is, however, a varying level of preparedness for operational disruptions across the financial system," the RBA said. "In an environment of rapid technological change, increased concentration, rising interconnectedness and heightened geopolitical risk, maintaining and building operational resilience will require ongoing vigilance across the financial system. The RBA added capital and liquidity resilience must be maintained. "It is important that lending standards remain sound in the face of continued strong competition in lending so that resilience is not eroded in an environment more prone to shocks," the RBA said. "The superannuation sector has been an important source of resilience and stability in the broader financial system over the years, but ongoing work to strengthen liquidity risk management practices is warranted as the sector continues to grow in size and as a larger share of superannuation balances become accessible to members."

items.title: MLC Super cuts admin, investment fees
items.teaser: MLC Super will cut administration and investment fees for members from October 1, with 511,000 members set to benefit from lower costs across its superannuation options.
items.brief_text: MLC Super will cut administration and investment fees for members from October 1, with 511,000 members set to benefit from lower costs across its superannuation options. The annual member administration fee will fall 23% from $78 to $60, reducing the fixed cost from $1.50 to $1.15 a week for eligible members. Investment fees and costs will also fall across MLC Super's MySuper and Simple Choice options, with reductions of up to 0.07 percentage points a year. MLC Super's flagship MySuper Growth portfolio, its largest option by funds under management, will see its investment fee fall from 0.69% to 0.67%, a year. The MLC High Growth option will also fall, from 0.85% to 0.83%. Members invested in some MLC Fixed Interest and Property options will also see lower buy-sell spreads, with Fixed Interest spreads falling to 0.10% for both purchases and sales from 0.15% and 0.20% respectively. Property spreads will fall from 0.30% for both purchases and sales to 0.20%. MLC super chief executive Dave Woodall said the changes were intended to leave more members' money invested for retirement. "We've reduced the headline fee, brought down a range of investment costs and made it cheaper for members to transact," Woodall said. "Every dollar a member doesn't pay in fees is a dollar that stays in their account, compounding over their working life, to help grow their superannuation balance and give them confidence in retirement." MLC super said most members would save $18 a year in administration fees, while a member with a $250,000 accumulation balance invested in MLC MySuper would save an average of $68 a year. The changes will also simplify how members and employers make contributions, with members moving to direct debit and PayID, while employers will use Superstream. "Confidence in super is built on people understanding what they are paying, what they are invested in and what it means for them," Woodall said. "Collectively, these changes improve value for members while reinforcing our commitment to maintaining a competitive, efficient and contemporary product suite."

items.title: Communication the weak link for advisers serving wealthy clients
items.teaser: A wealthy client can be happy with their returns and have every faith in their adviser’s technical skill, yet still feel they are not hearing enough from them, and new research has found that is the one part of the relationship where even the most satisfied want more.
items.brief_text: A wealthy client can be happy with their returns and have every faith in their adviser’s technical skill, yet still feel they are not hearing enough from them, and new research has found that is the one part of the relationship where even the most satisfied want more. Praemium and CoreData’s Rich Decisions study of high-net-worth (HNW) investors, those with more than $1 million to invest outside of super and the family home, found that communication recorded the lowest satisfaction result of any part of the advice experience, even though 84 per cent of advised clients were still satisfied with it. “Technical competency establishes credibility, but trust is sustained or lost through how an adviser communicates, especially when markets are volatile,” Praemium chief commercial officer Denis Orrock said. Clients said an adviser’s worth came down to how accessible and proactive they were, particularly when markets turned, while perceived neglect or a lack of honesty about performance could sour things fast. Just over a third (35 per cent) of advised HNW investors named strong communication as a “nice-to-have”, and a further 28 per cent said it was essential. Fees, on the other hand, barely came into it, with just 14 per cent saying competitive pricing was a must, compared with 39 per cent who wanted a genuinely personalised approach and 38 per cent who wanted a clear investment strategy with strong justification for decisions. That lines up with what advisers are already selling, with Praemium and CoreData research last year finding 85 per cent of HNW advisers said a personalised approach was central to their pitch. Praemium itself has been leaning into the HNW space, lifting funds under administration (FUA) by 21 per cent to $77.9 billion in the 2025-26 financial year off the back of $1.9 billion in net flows. Tax and estate planning was the biggest drawcard for HNW investors seeking advice at 53 per cent, but plenty were after something less tangible, with peace of mind (47 per cent), access to expertise they didn’t have (46 per cent) and an objective sounding board (43 per cent) not far behind. Orrock said these are financially knowledgeable investors who stay closely involved in their wealth and are not looking to hand over every decision. “What they value is an adviser they trust, who understands their circumstances and gives them greater confidence in the choices they make,” he said. CoreData chief executive Andrew Inwood added: “What stands out is that these investors aren’t outsourcing confidence, they’re supplementing it.” “This is a segment that knows its own mind and wants an adviser who adds to it, with real technical depth where it counts, someone to test their thinking, and a strategy explained clearly enough to stay engaged with. The advisers who grasp that distinction are the ones who keep these clients. Those in an ongoing advice relationship were also the happiest with where their money sat, with 84 per cent pleased with their investments, compared with 70 per cent of those who’d had one-off advice and 64 per cent of those going it alone. Advisers and wealth managers topped the list of most trusted financial professionals among HNW investors at 65 per cent, and among those already advised, 83 per cent had high trust in their adviser’s professional competency. There is still more advisers could be doing, according to the research, with clients who wanted extra support pointing first to tax planning and minimisation (40 per cent), followed by more regular or in-depth portfolio reviews (33 per cent), SMSF and superannuation strategy (31 per cent) and help preparing the next generation for inheritance (30 per cent). “The advisers who win this segment will be the ones who stay accessible, proactive and transparent,” Orrock said.

items.title: New entrants drive Q1 FAR growth
items.teaser: The slight retraction in adviser numbers this week hides a more substantial loss in experienced advisers as new entrants continue to be the main contributor to growth.
items.brief_text: The slight retraction in adviser numbers this week hides a more substantial loss in experienced advisers as new entrants continue to be the main contributor to growth. ASIC’s Financial Adviser Register (FAR) fell by net seven in the week ending 1 October, bringing the total down to 15,162 and marking one of just three weeks with net losses in FY2026-27 so far, according to Padua Wealth Data. This strong growth has largely been upheld by new entrants, with the same playing out this week as 14 hit the FAR, meaning that there were actually 21 experienced advisers leaving the register during this period. Looking back over the first quarter of FY27, there have been 192 new entrants since the week ending 2 July. Over that same period, the FAR has increased by net 178, suggesting there has actually been a net loss of 14 experienced advisers. At the same time, there has been a net increase of 16 licensees with 40 commencing and 24 ceasing, including two on either side this week, and Padua Wealth Data has recorded 1,394 appointments or resignations by advisers during this three-month period, with 70 occurring this past week. The calendar year is sitting at a net growth of 106 advisers, a significant uptick on this time last year where there was a net loss of 39 recorded over the same nine-month period which Padua Wealth Data founder Colin Williams attributed in part to advisers returning throughout 2026 after completing additional education requirements that kicked in on 1 January. Focusing on licensee shifts, there was only moderate movement by advisers this week with Lifespan reporting a net gain of two, both of which joined from Rhombus Enterprises’ RI Advice Group. One of this week’s new licensees, Michael Patman, kicked off with two advisers switching from The G & A Hunter Family licensee. A tail of 16 licensee were up by net one adviser each, including Macquarie Group, Morgans Group and Koda Capital. At the other end, Rhombus Enterprises was down by net four advisers this week including the two lost to Lifespan and another pair that are yet to be reappointed elsewhere. Endeavor Asset Management saw a net loss of three, all of which are yet to find a new home, and Findex Group and Centrepoint Group were both down by net two advisers each. The G & A Hunter Family Trust was down by net two. A tail of 16 licensees were down by net one adviser each, including Count Limited, Canaccord Group and Bell Financial Group.
